title: d-Matrix Raptor 3D-DRAM Accelerator for Generative Inference at Hot Chips 2026
gist: d-Matrix presented Raptor, an accelerator that stacks a TSMC N4 logic die directly on 3D DRAM to escape the HBM bandwidth ceiling of roughly 20 TB/s per package, claiming ~100 TB/s at 32GB per card, about 20x the bandwidth per square millimeter and 13.5x better mW per GB/s versus HBM4 parts. The talk detailed three entangled engineering problems (bank-to-channel mapping, I/O power, and 105C DRAM reliability) and the specific fixes for each.

themes.theme: Why SRAM and HBM both fail for frontier inference

insights.claim: KV cache scales with context length multiplied by batch size, so 64 users at 1M context can mean roughly 935 GB of KV cache, making inference simultaneously a capacity and a bandwidth problem.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies why long-context serving economics collapse without new memory architectures, driving the entire memory-attach investment thesis.
insights.quote: So 64 users at 1M context can mean roughly 935 GB of KV cache.
insights.locator: Model weights keep growing

insights.claim: A Corsair SRAM accelerator card pair reaches roughly 300 TB/s at about 1 ns latency but holds only about 4 GB, because a 6T SRAM cell is around 10 times larger than a DRAM cell and leakage runs to tens of watts at GB scale.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sets the hard physical limit on SRAM-only inference silicon, relegating that approach to draft models in speculative decoding.
insights.quote: A Corsair SRAM accelerator card pair reaches roughly 300 TB/s at about 1 ns latency, yet holds only about 4 GB.
insights.locator: SRAM meets the bandwidth target

insights.claim: SRAM-class accelerators are suitable for the draft model in speculative decoding rather than for holding frontier model weights, which STH suggests is how NVIDIA is using Groq.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reframes SRAM-accelerator businesses as components inside a larger serving stack rather than standalone GPU replacements.
insights.quote: This makes SRAM suitable for a draft model in speculative decoding, not for holding frontier model weights. That seems to be what NVIDIA is using Groq for as an example.
insights.locator: SRAM meets the bandwidth target

insights.claim: d-Matrix cites a practical bandwidth ceiling around 20 TB/s for HBM4 packages such as the NVIDIA Vera Rubin and AMD Instinct MI455, because pin speed and I/O width per base die improve slowly and package beachfront limits stacks to roughly 8-16 per package.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If 20 TB/s is a real package-level ceiling, HBM roadmaps cannot close the decode bandwidth gap and alternative memory architectures gain strategic value.
insights.quote: d-Matrix cites a practical bandwidth ceiling around 20 TB/s for HBM4 packages such as the NVIDIA Vera Rubin and AMD Instinct MI455.
insights.locator: HBM solves the capacity half

insights.claim: At 2.4 pJ/bit, pushing 100 TB/s through HBM consumes about 1.92 kW before any fabric traffic is counted, so packages today lack both the beachfront and the power budget to reach SRAM-class bandwidth with HBM.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Power, not just area, caps HBM scaling, which is why rack power budgets increasingly determine achievable inference bandwidth.
insights.quote: At 2.4 pJ/bit, pushing 100 TB/s through HBM eats about 1.92 kW before any fabric traffic is counted.
insights.locator: Bandwidth that high carries a power price

insights.claim: Vertical 3D IO costs around 0.3 to 0.4 pJ per bit, roughly 10 times lower than HBM's 2.5 to 5 pJ range, because it is a PHY-less millimeter-scale path rather than a centimeter-scale interposer route.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The energy-per-bit gap is the core economic argument for stacking compute on DRAM and the number to check against future HBM generations.
insights.quote: Vertical 3D IO comes in at around 0.3 to 0.4 pJ, about 10 times lower than HBM, because it is a PHY-less millimeter-scale path rather than a centimeter-scale interposer route.
insights.locator: 3D DRAM lands between the two extremes

insights.claim: Using fewer stacked layers than HBM means a larger die and better yield, inverting the usual assumption that more stacking is strictly better.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A yield-driven counterargument to the tall-stack HBM roadmap that could favor lower-cost manufacturing paths.
insights.quote: Fewer stacked layers than HBM also means a larger die and better yield.
insights.locator: 3D DRAM lands between the two extremes

insights.claim: d-Matrix says a 1-Hi logic-on-top stack held to no more than 0.5 W/mm2 can be liquid cooled while keeping the DRAM under 100 C, which is the thermal precondition for stacking compute on memory.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sets the specific power-density budget any logic-on-DRAM design must meet, a testable constraint on competing claims.
insights.quote: d-Matrix says a 1-Hi logic-on-top stack at no more than 0.5 W/mm2 can be liquid cooled and keep DRAM under 100 C.
insights.locator: d-Matrix’s answer is to stack compute directly on top of DRAM dies

insights.claim: Raptor puts a TSMC N4 logic die on top of a 3D DRAM die using 36 um face-to-face stacking, a process d-Matrix describes as proven, low-cost, high-volume, and high-yield.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Using a mature node and mainstream bonding pitch lowers execution risk versus hybrid-bonding-dependent roadmaps.
insights.locator: d-Matrix’s specific implementation is called Raptor

themes.theme: Decode is where inference time and bandwidth go

insights.claim: Prefill processes many prompt tokens in parallel and is compute-throughput-bound, whereas decode produces one token at a time and is typically memory-bandwidth-bound, with MoE staying memory-bound even at modest batch sizes.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A reusable model for judging which accelerators fit which half of a disaggregated serving deployment.
insights.locator: d-Matrix is now mapping that view of technologies

insights.claim: Most inference wall-clock time is spent in the decode phase, so improving decode bandwidth improves overall inference performance more than adding compute.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Directs capital toward memory bandwidth rather than FLOPS when optimizing serving cost per token.
insights.quote: d-Matrix highlights that most inference time is spent in the decode phase, so improving decode bandwidth improves overall inference performance.
insights.locator: Since decode dominates wall-clock runtime

insights.claim: Attention can flip from memory-bound to compute-bound with high GQA and speculative decoding, so the bottleneck moves with the serving technique in use.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hardware chosen for one bottleneck can be stranded when software techniques shift the bottleneck, a real risk in single-purpose accelerators.
insights.locator: d-Matrix is now mapping that view of technologies

insights.claim: At 32GB per card with 4-bit weights and an 8-bit KV cache, a 72-card Raptor scale-up can host a frontier model such as Kimi K3 at 1M context inside a single rack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Single-rack frontier serving at 1M context is the deployment claim that would make Raptor commercially interesting to inference providers.
insights.locator: At 32GB per card, with 4-bit weights

themes.theme: Three entangled engineering problems and their fixes

insights.claim: d-Matrix frames bank mapping, I/O power, and thermal reliability as entangled challenges where a solution to any one constrains the design space of the other two.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Explains why logic-on-DRAM has not already been productized despite being architecturally obvious, a barrier-to-entry argument.
insights.quote: d-Matrix walks through three entangled challenges in bank mapping, I/O power, and thermal reliability, noting that a solution to any one constrains the design space of the other two.
insights.locator: Those four problems are not independent

insights.claim: d-Matrix's die has 840 banks, 768 after 72 spares, spread across 256 channels for just 3 banks per channel, so a 128B flit takes two accesses and fetches 192B, wasting about 33 percent of bandwidth near 33 TB/s.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete illustration that raw memory bandwidth numbers overstate usable bandwidth unless the access granularity math works out.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Challenge 1: The Overfetch Dilemma

insights.claim: Stream blocking shares one partial 32B access across three flits so four accesses at 96B feed three flits at 128B, driving overfetch to zero with no shifting network required.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Recovers roughly a third of bandwidth through scheduling rather than more silicon, the kind of design-level arbitrage that decides cost per token.
insights.quote: Overfetch drops to zero, every column access is used, and no shifting network is required.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Solution: Stream Blocking

insights.claim: Moving 100 TB/s at 0.37 pJ/bit works out to 296 W just for I/O, and conventional data bus inversion cannot be used because the single-cycle 256-bit 3D-DRAM link has no burst and no sideband pin to signal the inversion choice.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows how techniques inherited from HBM break when the physical link changes, an underappreciated cost of memory architecture transitions.
insights.quote: Moving 100 TB/s at 0.37 pJ/bit works out to 296 W just for I/O, and conventional DBI could save 20 percent.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Challenge 2: The I/O Power Wall

insights.claim: Stream flipping compares each flit to the previous one and inverts when needed, delivering the 20 percent DBI saving with a single metadata bit per flit at 0.8 percent overhead and no PHY change.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A near-free 20 percent I/O power reduction is the sort of margin that determines whether an accelerator fits inside a rack power envelope.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Solution: Stream Flipping Pinless DBI

insights.claim: DRAM retention drops from 32 ms at 85C to 4 ms at 105C, demanding 8 times more refresh, while a 1 percent fault rate across 840 banks threatens whole channels and a single weak channel can throttle an entire slice.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the reliability cliff that makes hot logic-on-DRAM hard, and why competitors may have passed on the approach.
insights.quote: Retention drops from 32 ms at 85C to 4 ms at 105C, demanding 8 times more refresh while ECC and scrub must keep up.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Challenge 3: DRAM Reliability at 105C

insights.claim: Interleaving ECC and DBI bits into the last columns of each subarray and pairing commodity ECC with a Reed-Solomon code means reading 16 to 32 times fewer rows, so the 8-times-more-frequent refresh costs only about 1.37 percent and bandwidth stays near 100 TB/s with under 1.4 percent loss.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows the thermal penalty can be engineered down to noise, removing the strongest objection to running DRAM at 105C.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Solution: Thermal-Aware Refresh & ECC

insights.claim: Bank chaining uses two physical mux levels so the chiplet's 72 spare banks can absorb faults anywhere on the die while keeping channels symmetric, avoiding the uneconomical alternative of discarding bonded dies.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Yield recovery on bonded stacks is where 3D-DRAM economics live or die; this is the mechanism to scrutinize.
insights.locator: d-Matrix Solution: Bank Chaining

themes.theme: Claimed results and the skeptic's questions

insights.claim: d-Matrix claims Raptor posts about 32.6 GB/s per mm2 against roughly 1.5 GB/s for HBM parts, around 20 times the bandwidth per square millimeter, and 2.96 mW per GB/s against 40 mW, a 13.5x improvement, in a comparison against HBM4 and NVIDIA Rubin R200.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If these vendor figures survive independent testing, they reset the memory-density and power baseline for inference accelerators.
insights.quote: Raptor posts about 32.6 GB/s per mm2 compared with roughly 1.5 GB/s for the HBM parts, around 20 times the bandwidth per square millimeter, and 2.96 mW per GB/s against 40 mW, a 13.5x improvement.
insights.locator: Now d-Matrix has what looks like a silicon-area comparison

insights.claim: Raptor's headline result claims roughly 1,000 tokens per second per user while serving a 3-trillion-parameter class model at 1M context.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The interactivity figure to benchmark against Vera Rubin and Helios rack claims for long-context agentic serving.
insights.quote: Raptor’s result claims roughly 1,000 tokens per second per user, serving a 3-trillion-parameter class model with 1M context.
insights.locator: Raptor’s result claims roughly 1,000 tokens per second per user

insights.claim: d-Matrix's thesis is that moderate per-card memory paired with high bandwidth wins in low-latency inference, rather than maximizing capacity per accelerator.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the capacity-maximizing designs of HBM-based accelerators, and a testable positioning bet.
insights.quote: d-Matrix’s thesis is that moderate per-card memory paired with high bandwidth wins in low-latency inference.
insights.locator: Raptor’s result claims roughly 1,000 tokens per second per user

insights.claim: STH flags the obvious skeptic's question of why incumbents like NVIDIA are not already stacking DRAM on logic, and notes the presentation offered little on drawbacks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A discipline check on adjacent-architecture pitches: absence of incumbent adoption usually signals an undisclosed constraint.
insights.quote: my first question is usually “why is everyone not using this?”
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: If 3D DRAM closes the memory bandwidth gap, it reshapes how accelerator vendors weigh capacity against bandwidth in AI systems.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Second-order risk to HBM demand forecasts if logic-on-DRAM proves out in volume.
insights.quote: If 3D DRAM closes the memory bandwidth gap, it reshapes how accelerator vendors weigh capacity against bandwidth in AI systems.
insights.locator: Final Words
